content:
One widely circulated critique says that the Quran took its early content and style from the Hanif poets Zayd ibn Amr and Waraqa ibn Nawfal and from the false prophet Musaylima, and that some of Zayd's poems appear in it word for word. The claim sounds specific, so it can be tested against dates and texts.

Below are five points: what is fair in the claim, what the sources say of Zayd and Waraqa, what Zayd's verses contain, when Musaylima lived and what he said, and what the opponents of Muhammad (peace be upon him) actually alleged in Mecca.

The strongest form of the claim runs like this: Arabia before Muhammad already had men who rejected idols and spoke of one God, so the Quran's message did not arrive from nowhere. That much is true, and the Islamic sources say so themselves. They call such men hanifs, a word the Quran applies first to Abraham (2:135; 3:67).[1] Ibn Ishaq names Zayd and Waraqa among those who left idol worship before Islam.[2]

Ismail al Faruqi, in his essay on Islam in the Historical Atlas of the Religions of the World, makes the same point from the Muslim side. Islam, he notes, names the hanifiyya, the tradition of the hanifs, as its predecessor and identifies itself with it (10:105; 2:135). The hanifs, in his account, were Arabs in good standing with their tribes, neither Jewish nor Christian, who rejected the cults of Arabia and professed the faith of Abraham. For that reason he holds that the parallels between Islam and the older religions prove neither borrowing from them nor development out of them.[3]

A shared theme is not a shared text, however. The claim needs three further steps: that the poems contain Quranic wording, that they came first, and that the Quran copied them. The next entries test each step. The Quran never presents itself as a message without precedent. It says that it confirms what came before (3:3) and that earlier prophets taught the same call to worship God alone (21:25).

The hanifs did not form a movement with a scripture or a creed. Ibn Ishaq names four men who left the idols of Mecca together, and they went separate ways: Waraqa became a Christian, Ubayd Allah ibn Jahsh later became a Christian in Abyssinia, Uthman ibn al-Huwayrith went to the Byzantine court and became a Christian there, and Zayd remained a seeker who followed no organised religion.[2] Four men with four outcomes cannot have supplied a single coherent source for the Quran.

Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl refused meat offered to idols and, according to the reports, saved baby girls from being buried alive. Al-Bukhari records that he met the Prophet before any revelation came, and that he did not live to see Islam.[4] Ibn Ishaq places his death in the years before the prophethood, near the time the Kaaba was rebuilt.[2] A man who died before the first revelation cannot have written the surahs revealed afterwards, and no source credits him with doing so.

Waraqa ibn Nawfal was a cousin of Khadija and a Christian who knew the scriptures. When Muhammad came to her after the first revelation, Khadija took him to Waraqa, who said that the angel who came to him was the same one who came to Moses. Al-Bukhari adds that Waraqa died soon afterwards and the revelation paused.[5] The report is itself the evidence a critic would use, and it shows Waraqa as a witness who confirmed Muhammad, not as an author of anything he recited. No verses of Waraqa that match the Quran are recorded in the early sources.

Al-Bukhari also preserves a scene from Zayd's last years. Asma bint Abi Bakr remembered seeing him standing with his back against the Kaaba, saying, "O people of Quraysh, by God, none of you follows the religion of Abraham except me."[4] The report shows a lonely figure without followers or texts, protesting against his people's idols. Waraqa, for his part, told Muhammad that he wished he could be young and alive when his people drove him out, which suggests that he expected the message to meet resistance, not that he had helped to shape it.[5]

The few lines attributed to Zayd are preserved by Ibn Ishaq and later literary collections. Their theme is submission of the speaker to a Lord whom the earth and the clouds obey, and a rejection of the gods of his people.[2] The theme matches the Quran's, and a reader may fairly say so. The wording does not. No passage of the Quran is a quotation of these lines, and the claim that they appear "verbatim" has no basis that a reader can check against the sources.

Two further points apply. Zayd's lines are poetry in metre, while the Quran denies that it is poetry (36:69; 69:41) and is not composed in the metres of Arabic verse. And these poems reach us through works written well over a century after Zayd, which is why historians of early Arabic poetry treat the exact wording of many pre-Islamic verses with caution. If anything, that caution weighs against the critique: a later transmitter could have shaped a monotheist's lines to sound Islamic, which would reverse the direction of influence the claim assumes.

The same question arises with another poet often cited by critics, Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt of Ta'if, a contemporary of the Prophet who opposed him and died around 631. Poems attributed to Umayya contain stories and phrases that closely resemble the Quran. Many scholars, Western and Muslim, have concluded that much of that material was composed or reworked after Islam and attributed to him, because it reflects the Quran's language too closely to be independent.[6] A resemblance that appears only in later collections cannot show what came first.

Musaylima, of the tribe of Banu Hanifa in Yamama, claimed to be a prophet in the last years of Muhammad's life, after the Prophet had already been preaching for two decades. He was killed in the battle of Yamama, fought against the forces of Abu Bakr in the year 11 or 12 after the Hijra (about 632 to 633).[7] The Quran's early surahs were revealed in Mecca long before he appeared, so he cannot have supplied their style. If any borrowing took place, the evidence points the other way: a rival who imitated what was already being recited.

The sayings attributed to him survive in historians such as al-Tabari, who were hostile to him. They are short rhyming lines, some of them about frogs, elephants and sowing, and they are presented in the sources as mockery of his claim.[7] Their authenticity is itself uncertain, as with any report of a defeated opponent preserved by his enemies. A critic may say that a hostile record proves nothing either way, and that is correct. It leaves the chronology standing, and the chronology is what decides the question. The name Hanifa belongs to a tribe and has no connection with the Hanifs of the first entry.

Ibn Ishaq preserves an exchange of letters that shows how Musaylima saw himself. He wrote to the Prophet, from "Musaylima the messenger of God to Muhammad the messenger of God", proposing that the earth be divided between them, half to each. The Prophet's reply quoted the Quran: "the earth belongs to God; He gives it as inheritance to whom He wills of His servants, and the outcome is for the righteous."[8] The exchange records a man claiming a share of a prophethood already established, which is the opposite of a source for it.

The Meccans who rejected Muhammad searched for a human source and said so openly. The Quran records one accusation: "only a human being teaches him." It answers that the man they hint at speaks a foreign tongue, while this recitation is in clear Arabic (16:103).[9] It also records the charge that these were "tales of the ancients" that others wrote down for him (25:4-5).[9] The commentators discuss who the foreign man was, and they differ.

What is absent is as telling as what is present. Zayd's poems were known in Mecca, since he had lived there and clashed with his own family. Had his lines been the source of the early surahs, the opponents had every reason to say so, and the sources record no such accusation. Neither is there a report of anyone, then or later, pointing to a Quranic passage and matching it to a line of Zayd. The Quran also issues a challenge to produce a comparable text (2:23; 17:88), and no one has been recorded as answering it with Zayd's verses.[10]

Musaylima was the one who tried. The sayings attributed to him were, in the view of the sources, his attempt to produce something like the Quran, and the Arabs of his own time found them ridiculous; even some of his followers are reported to have said that they knew he was a liar but preferred a liar of their own tribal group, Rabi'a, to a truthful man of Mudar, the group to which Quraysh belonged.[7] The episode is evidence that the challenge was taken up, and of how its first audience judged the result.

The bottom line

Arabia did hold men who rejected idols before Muhammad, and the Islamic sources admit it. That agreement in theme is real. The stronger claims do not follow from it: Zayd died before the revelation began, Waraqa is reported only as a witness, no passage of the Quran matches a line of either man, and Musaylima appeared late in the Prophet's life and was killed soon after his death.

Readers who weigh the question should ask for the actual verses set beside the actual passages. The shared theme of one God is what the Quran itself says earlier prophets taught.

Notes

  1. Quran 2:135; 3:67; 16:120.
  2. Ibn Ishaq, Sira (in the recension of Ibn Hisham), the account of the Hanifs and of Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl.
  3. Ismail R. al Faruqi, "Islam", in Ismail Ragi A. al Faruqi (ed.) and David E. Sopher (map ed.), Historical Atlas of the Religions of the World (New York: Macmillan, 1974), p. 237.
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Virtues of the Companions, the hadith of Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl. Sahih al-Bukhari 3826, report of Abdullah ibn Umar, in which the Prophet meets Zayd at the foot of Baldah before revelation came, and 3827 and 3828 (chapter "The report of Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl"), checked on sunnah.com; Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 7, pp. 142-143 (Shamela text), where Ibn Hajar says that Zayd sought tawhid and rejected idols but died before the mission. Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari (Shamela text), vol. 7, p. 143, states that Zayd sought tawhid and left idols but died before the prophethood, and that he protected baby girls from burial.
  5. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Beginning of Revelation, the account of Khadija and Waraqa. Verified on Shamela and sunnah.com: Bukhari 3 (Aisha), Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition, Shamela text), vol. 1, p. 22.
  6. On the poetry attributed to Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt and its authenticity, see the article "Umayya b. Abi 'l-Salt" in The Encyclopaedia of Islam, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1960–2004).
  7. Al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wa al-Muluk, the accounts of Musaylima and the battle of Yamama. Tabari, Tarikh al-rusul wa-l-muluk (Shamela text), vol. 3, pp. 284 and 300: the rhyming sayings (the frog, the sowers and the black sheep) and Abu Bakr's reaction to the saying about the frog, "this is speech that did not come from a god or from piety".
  8. Ibn Ishaq, The Life of Muhammad, trans. A. Guillaume, pp. 649–650; Quran 7:128.
  9. Quran 16:103; 25:4-5; with the classical commentaries of al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir on those verses.
  10. Quran 2:23; 17:88; 36:69; 69:41.
